title: Biophysical Normalization and Trajectory Inference
markdown: ## What this covers This chapter opens Meichen Fang's 2025 Caltech thesis, *A biophysical approach to normalization and trajectory inference in single-cell RNA sequencing data analysis*. It sets out the question the whole thesis answers — how should single-cell RNA-seq counts be modeled so that removing technical noise and reconstructing a cell's position along a biological process both rest on a mechanism rather than a convenient statistical fix — and gives a first look at the two pieces of work built to answer it. It assumes only that the reader knows single-cell RNA-seq produces a matrix of digital (UMI) transcript counts, one row per gene and one column per cell; the technical detail of each project is left to later chapters. **A note on the source.** The file supplied for this chapter is the thesis's title page, followed — apparently by an artifact of how the source PDF was split during conversion — by a fragment of the Results sections of later chapters rather than by the thesis's own introductory prose. What follows is reconstructed from that fragment together with the thesis's own retrospective framing of itself, given in the Discussion of its trajectory-inference chapter and in its closing Future Directions chapter. It is not a paraphrase of a stated introduction, because none was present in the material converted for this chapter; see Sources for exactly what came from where. ## A thesis about two problems *A biophysical approach to normalization and trajectory inference in single-cell RNA sequencing data analysis*, by Meichen Fang, was defended May 28, 2025, for the degree of Doctor of Philosophy in Biological Engineering at Caltech. The title names its two problems directly. **Normalization** is the step, taken before almost any other analysis, of correcting each cell's counts for technical variation in how much of its RNA was actually captured and sequenced — one cell's library might simply have more total counts than another's for reasons that have nothing to do with biology. The standard fix is to divide by a per-cell size factor estimated from the total count, or something like it. **Trajectory inference** is the problem of recovering, from cells that were each sequenced once and destroyed, an ordering along some continuous process — differentiation, the cell cycle — that no single cell's measurement can show by itself. The standard fix builds a neighbor graph over cells and reads off an ordering heuristically. Both fixes work, in the sense that they are widely used. The thesis's complaint about both is the same: the correction is convenient rather than principled, and its output — a size factor, a pseudotime coordinate — carries no claim about what actually produced the counts. Its alternative, in both cases, is to write down a stochastic model of how transcription, splicing and degradation actually generate the counts, and fit *that* model to the data directly, so that the corrected quantity is a parameter with a physical meaning rather than a normalization convenience. ## Two cultures, held together The framing the thesis gives for this choice, in its closing chapter, is Leo Breiman's distinction between two cultures of statistical modeling (Breiman, 2001): **algorithmic models**, which fit flexible, often black-box functions for prediction without committing to a mechanism, against **data models**, which assume a generative process and estimate parameters that are supposed to mean something about the system that produced the data. Most of single-cell analysis, on this reading, sits in the algorithmic culture — clustering, nearest-neighbor graphs, dimensionality reduction — because it is cheap to run and does not require committing to a model of the underlying biology. The thesis's stated position is not that the algorithmic culture is wrong, but that the two should be used in sequence rather than in competition: explore a dataset first with algorithmic models, which give a broad, assumption-light overview; use what that overview suggests to build a mechanistic (data) model of the specific biological process at hand; and then let the mechanistic understanding inform a better-targeted algorithmic model, repeating the cycle as needed. Both projects in the thesis sit in the middle step of that cycle — each is a deliberate trade of some of an algorithmic model's flexibility for parameters that are supposed to be biophysically interpretable, and for a principled statistical account of how much to trust them. ## Case one: what looks like generic noise sometimes is not The first project addresses normalization by modeling **extrinsic noise** — the part of a cell's count variability that acts on many genes at once (as opposed to **intrinsic noise**, the gene-by-gene fluctuation of transcription itself). The approach singles out genes whose count variability across cells looks like plain Poisson sampling noise with no extra, shared component ("Poisson" genes), and uses the total count summed over just those genes, per cell, as an estimate of a cell-level scaling factor — the mechanistic analogue of a size factor. Two findings from this work stand out as evidence for treating this factor as more than a normalization trick: - Estimated this way, the scaling factor tracks systematically with **cell-cycle phase** in mouse embryonic stem cells with independently inferred cycle stage (Figure 3.9f). What is usually lumped into "technical noise" turns out, at least in part, to be a real biological quantity — cell size — varying in a way that a single scalar factor can actually capture, and the extrinsic noise level itself did not depend on a gene's mean expression (Figure 3.9a), consistent with treating it as a property of the cell rather than of individual genes. - The approach breaks in a **heterogeneous** population. Applied to a mixed PBMC dataset (T cells, NK cells, B cells, monocytes), the sum of "Poisson"-gene counts stopped tracking the total count sum well (Figure 3.9j), because different cell types carry different fractions of their transcriptome in a handful of highly expressed, cell-type-specific marker genes. A single global size factor, mechanistic or not, is the wrong tool once a dataset mixes cell types with genuinely different expression programs. ## Case two: Chronocell — fit a dynamical model, then ask whether to believe it The second project, and the one the thesis calls **Chronocell**, addresses trajectory inference. Rather than building a neighbor graph, it fits a small number of discrete cell states connected in a sequence, with piecewise-constant transcription rates within each state, directly to a cell's unspliced (nascent) and spliced (mature) RNA counts under a Poisson noise model. Fitting returns not a single pseudotime per cell but a **posterior distribution over process time** — the model's own statement of how confident it is about where a given cell sits. That posterior, together with model-comparison diagnostics, is the thesis's answer to a problem it treats as central: a snapshot dataset may simply not contain enough information to support a trajectory at all, and a method that always outputs an ordering regardless is not distinguishing a real signal from an artifact of the algorithm. Chronocell is fit from 100 random initializations and from bootstrap resamples, and the resulting spread of AIC scores and of the correlation between independent fits (summarized as an "average precision", AP) is read as evidence for or against the dataset supporting a trajectory. The same states, refit without an imposed ordering, give a Poisson-mixture clusters model to compare against as a null. Four real datasets illustrate the range of outcomes: - **PBMC T cells** — AIC is lower for the trajectory model, but 100 random initializations land on many different, similarly-scoring orderings (AP 0.28). The clusters model is judged more suitable; this dataset is a negative control that shows the diagnostic doing its job (Figure 4.20). - **Human forebrain** (glutamatergic neuronal lineage, La Manno et al., 2018) — reversed-direction orderings score comparably, and the average posterior concentrates almost entirely on the starting state, both signs that the dataset does not contain enough dynamical information to be ordered at all (Figure 4.21). - **Mouse erythroid lineage** during gastrulation (Pijuan-Sala et al., 2019) — AIC has a single, clear minimum in the biologically correct direction, AP is 0.79, and the recovered process time tracks real embryonic time from around E7.5 onward, matching when erythroid differentiation is understood to begin (Figures 4.22–4.23). The genes with the largest fitted change in transcription rate across states include several with independent literature support for a role in erythroid development. - **RPE1 cells across the cell cycle** (metabolically labeled, Battich, Beumer, et al., 2020) — fit with the constraint that the first and last states coincide, the posterior recovers a genuinely cyclic ordering (visualizable as a circle on a torus), and the three fitted intervals correspond to recognizable cell-cycle phases. As a further check, fitted **degradation rates** for 84 selected genes were compared to independent estimates from two metabolic-labeling methods (scEU-seq and TimeLapse-seq); the agreement was of a similar magnitude to the agreement between those two independent experimental methods with each other — offered as evidence that Chronocell's parameters carry real biophysical content, not just curve-fitting flexibility. Compared against Slingshot, Monocle 3, diffusion pseudotime, and veloVI: on data simulated under Chronocell's own model, the other methods fail to recover the true ordering; on data simulated by an independent tool (dyngen), all methods capture the right qualitative trend, with Chronocell comparable to or better than the rest; and on real time-course neuron data, only Monocle 3 among the alternatives tracked the correct direction of time. ## What the models leave out The thesis is explicit, in its own Discussion and Future Directions chapters, that both models are deliberate simplifications, chosen to stay tractable rather than to be complete: - Chronocell's piecewise-constant transcription rates describe genes whose regulatory state switches fast and saturates, which is not realistic for genes with a transient, peaked response (Rabani et al., 2011). Splicing and degradation rates are held constant in time, reasonable for many genes but not all. Transcriptional bursting is left out entirely — there is no closed-form solution for it in this model — and the consequence is that the fitted distributions are under-dispersed relative to real data; the thesis notes this is resolvable in principle by solving the model numerically rather than analytically. - Even with these simplifications, the thesis is blunt that accurate inference already imposes strict requirements on the data (stable AIC, a concentrated posterior spread across the process, consistent bootstraps): the underlying problem is under-specified once latent process time and flexible transcription rates are both allowed to vary, and a more realistic model would face *more* stringent requirements, not fewer. - A choice the thesis flags as unresolved is how physical (experimental) time should be translated into an assumption about heterogeneity within a timepoint — whether all cells at one timepoint share exactly one process time (a delta distribution) or are spread over a range (exponential, uniform, or something else). Different choices give different answers, and no choice is argued to be the right default; it depends on what is already understood about the process being studied. - The extrinsic-noise model is likewise flagged as an oversimplification: a single random variable per cell is not a complete account of extrinsic variability even in the reduced representation the model uses. - Benchmarking trajectory-inference methods against each other is treated with real caution: each method encodes a different implicit model of what an ordering even means, so comparing outputs without independent ground truth risks comparing incompatible things — an "apples to oranges" exercise, in the thesis's words, unless the comparison is anchored to real experimental time, as in the erythroid and RPE1 datasets above. ## Designing the next experiment, not just collecting more data The thesis closes by drawing a general lesson from both projects: reproducibility in single-cell RNA-seq is usually judged by comparing *mean* expression levels across experiments, but on its argument this misses the point — the full distribution of counts, not just its average, is the real signature of a technical process, in the way that a constant of acceleration, not merely the fact that objects fall, is what characterizes gravity. Because a mechanistic model makes quantitative, falsifiable predictions, it can be used before an experiment is run, to decide which experiment is actually worth running — rather than simply collecting more data of the same kind. The thesis points to a **closed-loop framework** for this, developed alongside the extrinsic-noise work (Gorin, Vastola, Fang, et al., 2022): write down two or more competing mechanistic hypotheses, work out mathematically what each predicts, use that to identify the experiment that would best tell them apart, run it, and use the result to refine or reject a model. The thesis illustrates the mathematical half of this loop with two competing models of how a gene's transcription rate fluctuates over time — a gamma Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process and a Cox–Ingersoll–Ross process — but reports that the loop's experimental half, closing it with an actual designed experiment, was not completed as part of this work. A related closed-loop design has, however, already been carried out in fluorescence-based transcriptomics (Fox, Neuert, and Munsky, 2020), which the thesis cites as evidence that the approach is workable, not merely theoretical. The thesis's summary of its own position: even in an era of large datasets, not all data are equally informative, and a dataset's value depends on how well it is matched to the specific question at hand rather than on its size. A mechanistic model earns its keep, on this view, even before it is fit to anything — by telling you which experiment is worth running in the first place. ## Sources - Title, author, degree and defense date: front matter of `01-introduction.md`. - Extrinsic-noise / cell-size findings (Figures 3.9–3.11, including the K562, mESC and PBMC comparisons): the body of `01-introduction.md`, which — despite the filename — is a fragment of a later Results section rather than the thesis's stated introduction (see the note above). - Chronocell's fitting procedure, diagnostics (AIC, average precision, posterior entropy) and its results on PBMC T cells, human forebrain, mouse erythroid, and RPE1 cell-cycle data (Figures 4.18–4.25): the remainder of `01-introduction.md`. - The thesis's own summary of Chronocell, its assumptions and their consequences, the benchmark against Slingshot, Monocle 3, diffusion pseudotime and veloVI: `02-4-4-discussion.md` (Section 4.4, "Discussion"). - The "two cultures" framing, the closed-loop experimental-design argument, the physics-reproducibility analogy, and the CIR/gamma Ornstein–Uhlenbeck example (Figure 5.1): `04-chapter-5-future-directions.md` ("Chapter 5, Future Directions"). - Citations (Breiman, 2001; Gorin, Vastola, Fang, et al., 2022; Fox, Neuert, and Munsky, 2020; Rabani et al., 2011; and the datasets' own primary sources) checked against `05-bibliography.md`. - **Not contained in the supplied material**: the thesis's own Introduction chapter — its stated motivation, background and chapter outline — was not present in the files converted for this chapter; what is presented above is reconstructed from the thesis's retrospective self-description in its Discussion and Future Directions chapters instead. All mathematics above is described in words rather than reproduced as formulas, per the source's own disclaimer that its equations were extracted by a model from a PDF with no text layer and are unverified.
